What does this number mean?

Stage is the water surface height in metres above the gauge's own local reference point (“station datum”, mASD). It is not the depth of the river, and different gauges have different datums, so their numbers can’t be compared directly. “Normal” here means within the EA’s typical range for this gauge — useful context, but not a flood-warning threshold. Official warnings are issued separately by the Environment Agency.

Analysis

How the river is behaving

Five linked views of the recorded data. Hover for exact readings, drag the timeline handles to zoom, and download any dataset.

01

Multi-station comparison

Why compare in different ways? (station datums explained)
  • Stage — each gauge’s height above its own local datum. Raw numbers are not comparable between gauges.
  • Change — centimetres gained or lost since the start of the window. Good for comparing timing of rises.
  • % of typical range — 0% = EA typical low, 100% = EA typical high for that gauge. Datum-independent; the best like-for-like comparison.
  • Derived mAOD — stage + the EA “stage-scale datum”, which the EA API documents as the gauge’s datum on Ordnance Datum. Derived here, not published as a reading; useful for seeing the water surface fall downstream (e.g. over Diglis weir).

02

Level gauge

Latest reading against EA reference levels for the gauge.

03

Where each gauge sits in its typical range

Latest reading as % of the EA typical range. Click a bar to focus that station.

04

Rate of change

How fast the recorded level is rising (amber) or falling (blue), in centimetres per hour, from readings one hour apart.

Each bar compares a reading with the one closest to 60 minutes earlier (within 10 min). Missing readings leave gaps; values are not interpolated.

05

Rainfall and river level

Hourly rainfall at an EA rain gauge (hanging bars) above the river level. Rivers respond to rain over the whole catchment, often hours to days later.

Rain totals use only complete hours (all four 15-minute readings present); missing hours stay blank rather than zero. A single gauge measures rain at one point and does not represent the whole Severn catchment.
